title: Rivian Beats Revenue Estimates, Raises Delivery Outlook as R2 SUV Gains Traction
excerpt: The EV maker posted $1.66 billion in Q2 revenue, a 27% jump, while its mass-market R2 SUV drove higher delivery guidance and a path toward positive gross margins.
body:
• Rivian's Q2 revenue hit $1.66 billion, up 27% year-over-year, beating Wall Street's $1.51 billion estimate.
  • The company raised full-year delivery guidance to 65,000–70,000 vehicles and narrowed its adjusted EBITDA loss forecast.
  • The R2 SUV, priced around $58,000, is drawing a diverse buyer base including first-time EV owners, with positive gross margins expected in H2 2026.
  • Software and services revenue surged 37% to $515 million, with $308 million from the Volkswagen joint venture.

Rivian Automotive reported second-quarter results that handily topped expectations on Thursday, posting revenue of $1.66 billion—a 27% increase from $1.3 billion a year earlier and well ahead of the $1.51 billion analysts had forecast. The EV maker delivered 12,194 vehicles in the quarter, up from 10,661 in the year-ago period, and raised its full-year delivery outlook.

Shares rose roughly 2% in after-hours trading as the company simultaneously cut its capital spending projection and narrowed its loss guidance.

R2 Launch Shifts the Equation

Much of the optimism centers on the R2, Rivian's lower-priced SUV that began customer deliveries in June. Priced around $58,000—a sharp discount from previous Rivian models that frequently crossed six figures—the R2 is designed to compete directly with the Tesla Model Y and bring the brand into the mainstream.

"The product that would motivate someone to move from ICE to an EV hasn't existed until R2."

— RJ Scaringe, CEO, Rivian

Scaringe told Reuters that the conversion rate of R2 reservations to orders was "meaningfully above" internal projections for the Launch Edition. The company hosted a record number of R2 demo drives during the quarter, and CFO Claire McDonough told investors that Rivian expects positive gross margins on the R2 in the second half of 2026.

Lower-priced R2 variants are slated for later this year and into next year, which could widen the vehicle's appeal further.

Financials: Losses Narrow, Margins Improve

Rivian posted a gross profit of $179 million—an 11% margin—reversing a $206 million gross loss in the same quarter last year. The automotive segment still recorded a $36 million gross loss, but that marks a dramatic improvement from the $335 million loss a year earlier, even after absorbing roughly $100 million in R2 production ramp costs.

Net loss narrowed to $837 million from $1.15 billion. Adjusted loss per share came in at $0.47, down from $0.80 in Q2 2025.

The company tightened its full-year adjusted EBITDA loss guidance to $1.8–$2.0 billion, from a prior range of $1.8–$2.1 billion, and lifted delivery guidance to 65,000–70,000 vehicles from 62,000–67,000. Capital expenditure projections were trimmed to $1.7–$1.8 billion, down from $1.95–$2.05 billion.

Software Revenue Emerges as a Growth Engine

Beyond vehicle sales, Rivian's software and services segment generated $515 million in revenue, a 37% jump, with $308 million contributed by its joint venture with Volkswagen. The segment posted $215 million in gross profit at a 42% margin, underscoring its role as a higher-margin counterweight to the capital-intensive car business.

Rivian also launched its paid Autonomy+ driver-assistance subscription during the quarter, available at about $50 per month or $2,500 as an outright purchase. Scaringe said advanced assisted driving would be "a key differentiator" for future customers.

Bucking a Weak U.S. EV Market

Rivian's results stand out against a challenging backdrop. U.S. sales of all-electric vehicles fell nearly 30% year-over-year in June, according to Motor Intelligence data, following the expiry of the $7,500 federal EV purchase tax credit in September 2025. Americans bought roughly 247,000 all-electric cars in Q2, down 21% from a year earlier, per Barron's.

Pure-play EV makers fared better than legacy automakers pivoting to electric. Tesla's global Q2 deliveries jumped 25%, while Ford and General Motors saw U.S. EV sales drop roughly 41% and 37%, respectively. The disappearance of the credit appears to have reshuffled buyer behavior rather than uniformly depressing demand.

What's Next

Rivian is building a new factory in Georgia slated to produce the R2 and other models starting in 2028, a bet on continued demand growth for its mass-market lineup. In the nearer term, the company's ability to sustain R2 momentum—and hit positive automotive gross margins—will be closely watched by investors when Q3 numbers arrive.

"We've been very positively encouraged by the conversion rate of reservations to orders for the Launch Edition. It is meaningfully above our own internal projections."

— RJ Scaringe, CEO, Rivian

With regulatory credit revenue dwindling amid U.S. policy changes, Rivian's path forward hinges on the R2's commercial success and the scaling of its software business—two pillars that Thursday's results suggest are gaining real traction.
nri_angle: Rivian's strong quarter and growing software business—bolstered by its Volkswagen joint venture—signal opportunities for investors tracking the EV sector's evolution amid shifting U.S. policy.
author: Diaspora Desk
